distractors: A neutral party brought in to settle a dispute between two sides who cannot resolve it themselves.
Someone senior who advises you in private, meeting you regularly to talk through your career and how to handle a difficult room.
A person appointed to test a proposal by arguing against it, so the weaknesses surface before a committee finds them. The opposition is assigned rather than sincerely held.

A colleague asked to give an account of your work to a panel deciding on a promotion, describing what they actually saw you do. What they contribute is evidence about the past, not pressure on the decision.

The senior person whose budget carries a piece of work and who answers to the board for whether it lands. It is a role defined by ownership of the money and the outcome, and it is usually written down somewhere on an org chart.
To put a question to a formal vote so that the room goes on record, rather than settling it in conversation.
To set out both sides of a question evenly so a committee can choose, keeping your own preference deliberately out of it.
To carry out a decision you argued against once it has been taken, and to defend it outside the room as though it were your own. It is a discipline a committee expects, not a view you hold.

To sign off formally on something another team has proposed so that the work can proceed. The act is authority exercised at a gate, and it says nothing about whether you would have chosen it yourself.

To keep raising the same point in successive meetings until the objections stop being made, on the theory that persistence eventually reads as agreement. It describes a tactic for wearing a room down rather than the strength of anything actually said.
